docs.title: Trusted Computing Base (TCB)
docs.text:
LRL employs a strict separation between Trusted and Untrusted components to minimize the attack surface for critical bugs.

Component Trust Level Role kernel crate Trusted The only code that must be correct for logical soundness. If the kernel has a bug, proofs may be unsound. frontend Untrusted Parses and elaborates code. Bugs cause compile errors, not false proofs. codegen Untrusted Generates Rust/MIR. Bugs may cause runtime crashes, not unsound proofs. cli Untrusted User interface only.

docs.title: Kernel Guarantees (P1–P8)
docs.text: These are the release bar promises that the kernel enforces. Every release is validated against these guarantees.

docs.title: P1: Kernel Boundary Enforcement
docs.text:
All definitions and expressions are re-checked by the kernel before acceptance. No production path can bypass kernel validation.

What this means: Even if the elaborator or frontend has bugs, the kernel acts as a final gatekeeper. Malformed or unsound terms are rejected.

docs.title: P2: Totality Boundary
docs.text:
• def forbids general recursion (fix) and partial constructs (non-terminating code).
  • partial def is the only place where general recursion is allowed.
  • Partial constructs cannot appear in types or definitional equality checks.

What this means: Proofs and type-level computations are guaranteed to terminate. Only explicitly marked partial def can contain potentially non-terminating code.

docs.title: P3: Prop/Erasure Safety
docs.text:
• Prop-like types are correctly classified (including opaque aliases).
  • Large elimination from Prop into runtime data is forbidden (unless explicitly allowed).
  • Proof erasure cannot be bypassed via aliasing or opaque wrappers.

What this means: Proofs are computationally irrelevant at runtime. You cannot accidentally leak proof terms into executable code.

docs.title: P4: Macro Boundary & Hygiene
docs.text:
• The macro boundary Deny works after full expansion (including quasiquote) and cannot be bypassed.
  • Hygiene behavior matches the documented policy—macros cannot accidentally capture or shadow user bindings.

What this means: Macros are sandboxed. A macro cannot smuggle unsafe constructs past the boundary, and variable capture is controlled.

docs.title: P5: Borrow/Lifetime Safety (MIR/NLL)
docs.text:
• MIR-level borrow checking rejects aliasing, deref, and projection errors.
  • Lifetime labels are not laundered across kernel/MIR boundaries.
  • MIR lowering does not erase types in ways that bypass borrow/move/copy enforcement.

What this means: Memory safety is enforced at the MIR level, similar to Rust's borrow checker. Use-after-free and data races are caught before code generation.

docs.title: P6: Axiom/Noncomputable Policy
docs.text:
• Logical axioms (like classical logic) require noncomputable or unsafe markers.
  • Runtime primitives are not misclassified as logical axioms.
  • Macro boundaries cannot smuggle axioms into the prelude under Deny.

What this means: You always know when you're using axioms that might affect logical consistency or computability.

docs.title: P7: Interior Mutability Policy
docs.text:
• If RefCell/Mutex runtime checks are not implemented, safe usage must be gated or forbidden.
  • If enabled, runtime checks are actually emitted (no silent no-ops in "safe" mode).

What this means: Interior mutability follows Rust's model—either the compiler proves safety, or runtime checks enforce it. There are no silent gaps.

docs.title: P8: Definitional Equality Fuel/Transparency
docs.text:
• Fuel exhaustion is diagnosable and never misreported as success.
  • Opaque/transparency behavior matches documented policy.

What this means: When the type checker gives up on proving equality (due to computation limits), it tells you clearly instead of silently accepting or rejecting.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A collection of examples demonstrating LeanRustLisp's capabilities.

docs.title: 1. Natural Numbers & Recursion
docs.text:
Demonstrates inductive types and structural recursion.

(inductive Nat (Type 0)
  (zero Nat)
  (succ (-> Nat Nat)))

(def add (-> Nat Nat Nat)
  (lam n (lam m
    (match n
      (zero m)
      (succ (pred) (succ (add pred m)))))))

Key Concept: The kernel verifies that add terminates because pred is a structural sub-term of n.

docs.title: 2. Safe Array Access (Dependent Types)
docs.text:
Demonstrates dependent types for bounds checking.

;; Vector of length n
(inductive Vec (Type 0) (Nat)
  (nil (Vec zero))
  (cons (forall (n : Nat) (-> Nat (Vec n) (Vec (succ n))))))

;; Safe lookup (impossible to call with out-of-bounds index)
(def lookup (forall (n : Nat) (-> (Fin n) (Vec n) Nat))
  ...)

Key Concept: The type system prevents out-of-bounds errors at compile time.

docs.title: 3. hygienic Macros
docs.text:
Demonstrates the macro system.

(macro unless (cond body)
  `(if (not ,cond) ,body ()))

(unless (is-empty list)
  (process list))

Key Concept: Macros transform syntax before elaboration. Hygiene ensures variables don't capture accidentally.

docs.title: 4. Borrowing & Ownership
docs.text:
Demonstrates affine types and borrow checking.

(def process (-> (Ref String) Unit) ...)

(let s "hello")
(process (borrow s)) ;; OK: borrow
(consume s)          ;; OK: move
;; (process (borrow s)) ;; ERROR: Use after move

Key Concept: Linear resources must be used exactly once (or borrowed).

docs.title: 5. Noncomputable Logic
docs.text:
Demonstrates erasure and logical axioms.

(axiom classical_choice ...)

(def my_theorem (-> Prop Prop)
  (lam p (or p (not p)))) ;; Uses classical logic

;; (eval my_theorem) ;; ERROR: Cannot evaluate noncomputable definition

Key Concept: Logical proofs are erased at runtime and cannot pollute executable code.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: Why LeanRustLisp? Here are the problems we solve.

docs.title: Verified Systems Programming
docs.text:
Problem: C/C++ are unsafe. Rust is safe but hard to verify formally.

Solution: LRL allows you to write low-level code with integrated proofs of correctness.

Status: Planned

docs.title: Safe High-Performance Infrastructure
docs.text:
Problem: High-performance code often requires unsafe in Rust.

Solution: Dependent types can express invariants (like buffer sizes or state machine transitions) that remove the need for runtime checks without unsafe.

Status: Early Access

docs.title: DSLs and Tooling
docs.text:
Problem: Creating a new language is hard.

Solution: LRL's Racket-like macro system makes it a "language for building languages."

Status: Available

docs.title: Security-Sensitive Capability Code
docs.text:
Problem: Access control is often implicit.

Solution: Linear capability tokens (IO, Network) enforce security policies at the type level.

Status: Designing

docs.title: Proof-Carrying APIs
docs.text:
Problem: APIs rely on documentation for constraints ("must call init first").

Solution: Types encode the protocol. A function strictly cannot be called in the wrong state.

Status: Available

docs.title: Research & Education
docs.text:
Problem: PL research languages are often slow or garbage collected.

Solution: LRL provides a playground for type theory that compiles to standard, fast systems code.

Status: Available

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
LeanRustLisp (LRL) is an experimental programming language designed to unify three powerful concepts:

  1. Lean-grade Specification: Using dependent types and inductive families to specify precise program behavior and prove correctness.
  2. Rust-grade Resource Discipline: Using affine types, ownership, and borrow checking to manage memory and resources safely and efficiently without garbage collection.
  3. Lisp-grade Extensibility: Using S-expressions and hygienic macros to allow the language to be extended and programmed by the user.

docs.title: Systems Performance
docs.text: LRL aims to be a systems language. By adopting Rust's ownership model, it avoids the runtime overhead of a garbage collector, making it suitable for real-time and resource-constrained environments.

docs.title: Correctness
docs.text: With a core calculus based on the Calculus of Inductive Constructions (CIC), LRL allows you to express complex invariants in your types. You can write proofs that your code satisfies these invariants, and the compiler checks them.

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text: The "Lisp" in the name isn't just about parentheses. It's about the philosophy that the language should be programmable. Macros allow you to define new syntactic forms that desugar into core concepts, making the language adaptable to your domain.

docs.title: Three Small Examples
docs.text:
;; 1) Correctness: proof checked by type checker.
(def zero-is-zero (Eq Nat zero zero)
  (refl Nat zero))

;; 2) Resource discipline: borrowing is explicit.
(noncomputable shared-borrow (pi x Nat Nat)
  (lam x Nat
    (let r (Ref #[r] Shared Nat) (& x)
      x)))

;; 3) Extensibility: syntax transformation via macro.
(defmacro mk-inc (v)
  (quasiquote (add (unquote v) (succ zero))))

(def demo Nat (mk-inc (succ zero)))

These examples illustrate a recurring theme in LRL: strong static guarantees with straightforward runtime behavior.

docs.title: What LRL is NOT
docs.text:
• A Dynamic Scripting Language: While it looks like Lisp, it is statically typed and compiled.
  • A General Proof Assistant: While it has proof capabilities, the focus is on verifying software, not general mathematics (though it shares the same foundations as Lean/Coq).
  • Finished: LRL is currently in Alpha.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To build LeanRustLisp (LRL), you need the standard Rust toolchain installed: 1. rustc 2. cargo

If you don't have these, install them via rustup.rs.

docs.title: Building from Source
docs.text:
Clone the repository and build the workspace:

git clone https://github.com/Kendiukhov/LeanRustLisp
cd LeanRustLisp
cargo build

The compiled binaries will be in target/debug.

docs.title: Running the REPL
docs.text:
The easiest way to explore LRL is the Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL).

cargo run -p cli

You should see a prompt: 

LRL>

Try typing a simple expression: 

LRL> (add 1 2)
3 : Int
// Result evaluation and type

docs.title: Running a File
docs.text:
To interpret an LRL file directly:

cargo run -p cli -- path/to/file.lrl

For example, try running one of the tests: 

cargo run -p cli -- tests/simple_test.lrl

docs.title: Your First Program: Hello World
docs.text: Let's write and understand a complete Hello World program in LRL.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the File
docs.text:
Create a new file called hello.lrl:

;; hello.lrl - Your first LRL program

(def entry Text
  (print "Hello, World!"))

The program defines a main entry point that prints a greeting.

docs.title: Step 2: Run It
docs.text:
cargo run -p cli -- compile hello.lrl
./build/output

You should see: 

Hello, World!

docs.title: Step 3: Understanding the Code
docs.text: Let's break down each element:

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
;; hello.lrl - Your first LRL program

Lines starting with ;; are comments. They're ignored by the compiler.

docs.title: String Literals
docs.text:
"Hello, World!"

Text enclosed in double quotes "..." is a string literal. LRL automatically converts this into a Text value.

docs.title: The Program Structure
docs.text:
(def entry Text
  (print "Hello, World!"))
  • def — Introduces a new definition
  • entry — The name of the definition (the last expression is evaluated)
  • Text — The return type (print returns the text it prints)
  • (print ...) — The body of the definition
  • print — A built-in function that outputs Text to the console

docs.title: A More Interesting Example
docs.text:
Let's create a program with multiple definitions:

;; greet.lrl - A greeting program

(def name Text "LRL User")

(def entry Text
  (print name))

Run it: 

cargo run -p cli -- compile greet.lrl && ./build/output

Output: 

LRL User

docs.title: Defining Values
docs.text:
(def name Text "LRL User")
  • def — Introduces a definition
  • name — The identifier
  • Text — The type (required)
  • "LRL User" — The value

docs.title: Printing Numbers
docs.text:
You can also print numbers directly:

;; numbers.lrl - Print some numbers

(def answer Nat (+ 2 3))
(print_nat answer)

Output: 

5

docs.title: Understanding Nat
docs.text:
• Nat — Natural numbers (0, 1, 2, ...)
  • + — Addition operator (prefix notation)
  • print_nat — Prints a natural number

LRL also supports signed integers (Int) and floating-point numbers (Float):

(def x Int (- 3 5))       ;; -2 (signed subtraction)
(def y Float (+f 1.5 2.5)) ;; 4.0 (float addition)

docs.title: Why S-Expressions?
docs.text:
You might wonder why LRL uses parentheses everywhere. This is called S-expression syntax (from Lisp). The benefits:

  1. Homoiconicity — Code is data, making macros natural
  2. Unambiguous parsing — No precedence rules to remember
  3. Easy to extend — Adding new syntax forms is trivial

Once you get used to it, (+ 1 2) reads just as naturally as 1 + 2.

docs.title: Compiling to Binary
docs.text:
To compile an LRL program to a standalone executable:

cargo run -p cli -- compile path/to/file.lrl -o my_program
./my_program

docs.title: Debugging and inspection
docs.text: LRL provides several flags to help you understand what the compiler is doing.

docs.title: Macro Expansion
docs.text:
To see how your macros expand, use specific flags. Note that you must provide a file argument.

  • --expand-1: Expands top-level macros one step.
  • --expand-full: Fully expands all macros.
  • --trace-expand: Shows the expansion process step-by-step.
cargo run -p cli -- --expand-1 path/to/file.lrl

docs.title: Trace Macros
docs.text:
To see macro expansion traces while running or compiling: 

cargo run -p cli -- --trace-macros path/to/file.lrl

docs.title: Definitional Equality Fuel
docs.text:
If you hit recursion limits during type checking, you can increase the "fuel" for the definitional equality checker: 

cargo run -p cli -- --defeq-fuel 1000000 path/to/file.lrl

docs.title: A Tour of LeanRustLisp
docs.text: This chapter takes you through a whirlwind tour of LRL's core features.

docs.title: 1. Defining Inductive Types
docs.text:
LRL uses inductive types to define data structures. Here is the classic definition of natural numbers.

(inductive Nat (sort 1)
  (ctor zero Nat)
  (ctor succ (pi n Nat Nat)))
  • Nat is the type name.
  • (sort 1) is its universe.
  • zero is a constructor that is a Nat.
  • succ is a constructor that takes a Nat and returns a Nat.

docs.title: 2. Defining Functions
docs.text:
We can define functions using def and lam (lambda).

(def one Nat (succ zero))

(def inc (pi n Nat Nat)
  (lam n Nat
    (succ n)))

docs.title: 3. Pattern Matching
docs.text:
We use match to deconstruct inductive types.

(def is-zero (pi n Nat Bool)
  (lam n Nat
    (match n Bool
      (case (zero) true)
      (case (succ m ih) false))))

Note: Bool, true, and false are defined in the standard prelude.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation
docs.text:
You can evaluate expressions in the REPL or at the top level of a file (which prints the result).

(is-zero zero)
;; Output: true : Bool

(is-zero (succ zero))
;; Output: false : Bool

docs.title: 5. Macro Expansion
docs.text:
Macros allow you to extend syntax at compile time. A simple example:

(defmacro plus_two (x)
  (quasiquote (add (unquote x) (succ (succ zero)))))

(def x Nat (succ zero))
(def y Nat (plus_two x))
;; Expands to: (add x (succ (succ zero)))

Macros operate on syntax objects (x is syntax) and return new syntax.

docs.title: 6. Dependent Types
docs.text:
LRL is dependently typed: types can mention values. Eq in the prelude is a simple indexed family.

(def zero-is-zero (Eq Nat zero zero)
  (refl Nat zero))

docs.title: 7. Positive Properties at a Glance
docs.text:
This small group of definitions shows three useful guarantees.

;; 1) Total structural recursion.
(def nat-pred (pi n Nat Nat)
  (lam n Nat
    (match n Nat
      (case (zero) zero)
      (case (succ n-prev ih) n-prev))))

;; 2) Hygienic macro expansion (no accidental capture).
(defmacro m1 (body) (lam x Nat body))
(def y0 Nat 10)
(def still-y0 Nat (app (m1 y0) 99)) ;; evaluates to 10

;; 3) Proof-carrying API: proof is checked statically.
(def with-self-eq
  (pi n Nat (pi p (Eq Nat n n) Nat))
  (lam n Nat
    (lam p (Eq Nat n n)
      n)))

(def checked-one Nat
  (with-self-eq (succ zero) (refl Nat (succ zero))))

The compiler checks each property (termination shape, hygiene, and proof typing) before runtime.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text: LRL uses S-expressions (symbolic expressions, or "sexprs") as its surface syntax. If you've used Lisp or Scheme, this will feel familiar. If not, don't worry—it's very simple.

docs.title: Atoms and Lists
docs.text: The code is made of atoms and lists.

docs.title: Atoms
docs.text:
• Integers: 0, 42, -123
  • Strings: "Hello world"
  • Symbols: foo, Nat, add, +
  • Keywords: There are a few reserved keywords like def, lam, match, but most "keywords" are just symbols that macros recognize.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text: A list is parentheses surrounding zero or more elements separated by whitespace. - () : The empty list (nil). - (add 1 2) : A list with three elements. - (lam x (sort 0) x) : Nested lists.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
Line comments start with ;. 

; This is a comment
(def x Nat zero) ; This is also a comment

docs.title: Lambda (lam)
docs.text:
Constructs an anonymous function. 

(lam parameter type body)
Example: 
(lam x Nat (succ x))

docs.title: Let (let)
docs.text:
Local bindings. 

(let x 1
  (add x x))
Note: let syntax might vary depending on macro definition in prelude, but conceptually it binds a value to a name in a scope.

docs.title: Definitions (def)
docs.text:
Top-level definitions bind a name to a value globally. 

(def name type value)
Example: 
(def my-num Nat (succ zero))

docs.title: Reading Error Messages
docs.text:
LRL tries to provide helpful error spans.

Error: Type mismatch
  --> my_file.lrl:10:5
   |
10 | (add true 1)
   |      ^^^^
   |
   = Expected type: Int
   = Found type: Bool

When macros are involved, the error might point to the expansion or the original source, depending on where the error was detected. Use --trace-macros if you are confused about where an error is coming form.

docs.title: Types and Terms
docs.text: In LRL, terms and types are unified (to an extent). However, there is a strict hierarchy of universes.

docs.title: Prop and Type
docs.text:
LRL distinguishes between logical propositions and computational data.

  • Prop: The universe of logical propositions. Elements of Prop are erased at runtime.
  • Type n: The universe of computational types at level n. Type 0 is the type of ordinary data types like Nat and Bool. Type 1 is the type of Type 0, and so on.

docs.title: Functions (Pi Types)
docs.text:
The type of a function is written as a Pi type (dependent product).

(pi (x A) B)

If B does not depend on x, this is a simple function arrow A -> B.

(-> Nat Nat)  ; Simple function
(pi (n Nat) (Vec Nat n)) ; Dependent function

docs.title: Dependent Types
docs.text: Dependent types allow types to depend on values. A classic existence proof is "safe vector access" or "vectors of a specific length".

docs.title: Example: Polymorphic Identity
docs.text:
(def id (pi (A (Type 0)) (-> A A))
  (lam A (Type 0) (lam x A x)))

(id Nat zero) 
;; A is explicitly passed as Nat

Note: In future versions, implicit arguments will make this less verbose.

docs.title: Definitional Equality
docs.text:
The type checker considers two terms equal if they reduce to the same normal form. This includes:

  • Beta (β) reduction: Applying a lambda (lam x t) u reduces to t[x/u].
  • Delta (δ) reduction: Unfolding a definition. id reduces to its body.
  • Iota (ι) reduction: Pattern matching reduction (e.g., match (succ n) reduces to the succ branch).

This means you don't need to manually prove that (add 1 2) equals 3. They are definitionally equal.

docs.title: Inductives and Matching
docs.text: Inductive types are the fundamental way to define data in LRL.

docs.title: Defining Inductives
docs.text:
Use the inductive form.

(inductive List (-> (Type 0) (Type 0))
  (nil (List A))
  (cons (-> A (List A) (List A))))
  • Parameters: List takes a parameter (Type 0) implicitly by the kind signature.
  • Constructors: list the constructors and their full types.

docs.title: Pattern Matching
docs.text:
The match expression allows you to branch on constructors.

(def length (-> (List Nat) Nat)
  (lam l (List Nat)
    (match l
      (nil zero)
      (cons h t (succ (length t))))))

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text: Recursive functions like length are allowed, but the kernel checks termination. The simplest form of termination is structural recursion on an inductive argument.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Missing Cases: All constructors must be covered.
  • Erasure: You cannot pattern match on a Prop (proof) to produce a Type (data) result. This is a fundamental restriction to ensure proofs can be erased.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
You've already seen def.

(def name type value)

Definitions are opaque if you mark them as opaque (future feature), but by default, they are transparent—the type checker can unfold them to see their value.

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Types/Inductives: CamelCase (e.g., Nat, List, MyType).
  • Functions/Values: kebab-case (e.g., add, is-valid, my-function).
  • Constructors: kebab-case or CamelCase depending on preference (stdlib usually uses lowercase for constructors like zero, succ, true, false).

docs.title: Modules (Planned)
docs.text:
LRL has a preliminary concept of modules based on files.

  • Each file is a module.
  • prelude is implicitly imported.

Note: The module system is currently under active development. Expect changes here.

docs.title: The Standard Library
docs.text:
The standard library is located in stdlib/.

  • stdlib/prelude_api.lrl: Shared public prelude contract (names/types/functions).
  • stdlib/prelude_impl_dynamic.lrl: Dynamic backend platform layer.
  • stdlib/prelude_impl_typed.lrl: Typed/auto backend platform layer.

User code should target the API contract, not backend-specific prelude files. Shared logic belongs in prelude_api.lrl; impl preludes are for backend-dependent runtime/platform wiring.

docs.title: Effects and IO
docs.text: LRL separates pure logic from side effects.

docs.title: The IO Effect
docs.text:
Conceptually, IO is not "just another value transform"; it marks interaction with the outside world.

Note: The effect system is still in early alpha. Currently, we largely model IO via monads, but a full algebraic effect system is planned.

docs.title: Purity
docs.text:
LRL, like Lean/Coq, is pure. A function Nat -> Nat always returns the same output for the same input and has no observable side effects.

(def double (pi n Nat Nat)
  (lam n Nat
    (add n n)))

docs.title: Current Alpha Surface
docs.text:
In current builds, common effectful operations are exposed through prelude functions such as print, read_file, and write_file.

(def echo-file Text
  (let contents Text (read_file "input.txt")
    (write_file "output.txt" contents)))

(def entry Text
  (print "Hello, world!"))

docs.title: Why separation?
docs.text:
Strict separation allows the compiler to erase proofs and pure computations that aren't needed at runtime, while guaranteeing that "safe" code doesn't accidentally wipe your hard drive.

It also gives a practical benefit today: the same source can be validated in a more pure/dynamic environment and then compiled on the typed backend where platform hooks perform real side effects.

docs.title: Ownership and Borrowing
docs.text: LRL adopts Rust's ownership model to manage memory without a garbage collector.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Every value in LRL has a single owner. When you pass a non-Copy value to a function, you move it, transferring ownership.

(inductive Resource (sort 1)
  (ctor acquire Resource))

(def use-resource (pi r Resource Nat)
  (lam r Resource zero))

(def create-and-use Nat
  (use-resource acquire))

docs.title: Copy Types
docs.text: Simple types like Nat and Bool are Copy. They are duplicated when passed, so the original remains usable.

docs.title: Borrowing
docs.text:
You can allow temporary access to a value via references.

  • &T: Shared (immutable) reference. Many allowed.
  • &mut T: Mutable reference. Only one allowed (exclusive).

Borrow-centric examples often use noncomputable because references are lowered by the MIR phase.

docs.title: The Rules of Borrowing
docs.text:
1. At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references.
  2. References must always be valid.

docs.title: Positive Example: Multiple Shared Borrows
docs.text:
(noncomputable use-shared (pi r (Ref #[r] Shared Nat) Nat)
  (lam r (Ref #[r] Shared Nat) zero))

(noncomputable shared-borrows-ok (pi x Nat Nat)
  (lam x Nat
    (let r1 (Ref #[r] Shared Nat) (& x)
      (let r2 (Ref #[r] Shared Nat) (& x)
        (use-shared r1)))))

This is accepted: multiple shared borrows can coexist.

docs.title: Positive Example: Branch-Local Borrows
docs.text:
(noncomputable use-mut (pi r (Ref #[r] Mut Nat) Nat)
  (lam r (Ref #[r] Mut Nat) zero))

(noncomputable branch-borrow-ok (pi x Nat (pi n Nat Nat))
  (lam x Nat
    (lam n Nat
      (match n Nat
        (case (zero)
          (let r (Ref #[r] Shared Nat) (& x)
            (use-shared r)))
        (case (succ k)
          (let m (Ref #[r] Mut Nat) (&mut x)
            (use-mut m)))))))

This is also accepted: borrows scoped inside separate match branches do not conflict.

docs.title: Rejected Example: Shared Then Mutable
docs.text:
(noncomputable borrow-then-mutate (pi x Nat Nat)
  (lam x Nat
    (let r (Ref #[r] Shared Nat) (& x)
      (let m (Ref #[r] Mut Nat) (&mut x)
        (use-shared r)))))

borrow-then-mutate is rejected: mutable and shared borrows overlap on the same value.

This discipline prevents data races and iterator invalidation at compile time.

docs.title: Macros and Metaprogramming
docs.text: LRL is a Lisp, so code is data. Macros allow you to transform code at compile time.

docs.title: Defining Macros
docs.text:
Use defmacro.

(defmacro mk-inc (val)
  (quasiquote (add (unquote val) (succ zero))))

Example use:

(def x Nat (succ (succ zero)))
(def y Nat (mk-inc x))
;; expands to: (add x (succ zero))

Macro expansion runs before type checking.

docs.title: Hygiene
docs.text:
LRL macros are hygienic. This means variables introduced by macros don't accidentally capture variables from the user's code, and vice versa.

(defmacro m1 (body) (lam x Nat body))
(def y Nat 10)
(def always-y (pi _ Nat Nat) (m1 y))
(def r1 Nat (app always-y 99)) ;; 10

(defmacro m2 () (lam x Nat x))
(def x Nat 5)
(def id-from-macro (pi _ Nat Nat) (m2))
(def r2 Nat (app id-from-macro 100)) ;; 100

(def z Nat 7)
(defmacro m3 () z)
(def r3 Nat (app (lam z Nat (m3)) 8)) ;; 7

In r1, the macro's internal binder does not capture y. In r2, call-site x does not capture the macro-generated x. In r3, local z does not capture macro z.

docs.title: Debugging Macros
docs.text:
If a macro behaves unexpectedly, inspect expansions:

cargo run -p cli -- --expand-1 my_file.lrl
cargo run -p cli -- --expand-full my_file.lrl
cargo run -p cli -- --trace-macros my_file.lrl

This gives a deterministic view of exactly what code the type checker receives.

docs.title: Proofs and Tactics
docs.text: LRL follows the Curry-Howard correspondence: Propositions are Types and Proofs are Programs.

docs.title: Propositions are Types
docs.text:
To prove a statement P, you define a type P and construct a term t : P.

;; Proposition: 0 = 0
(def zero-is-zero (Eq Nat zero zero)
  (refl Nat zero))

docs.title: Checked Proof Arguments
docs.text:
You can require proofs in APIs:

(def with-self-eq
  (pi n Nat (pi p (Eq Nat n n) Nat))
  (lam n Nat
    (lam p (Eq Nat n n)
      n)))

(def one Nat (succ zero))
(def one-is-one (Eq Nat one one)
  (refl Nat one))

(def checked-one Nat
  (with-self-eq one one-is-one))

checked-one only exists if the proof term type-checks.

docs.title: Proof Erasure
docs.text: Terms in Prop are erased at runtime. In practice, this means proof-heavy APIs can compile down to the same runtime behavior as proof-free equivalents.

docs.title: Why This Is Useful
docs.text:
• You can enforce invariants statically.
  • You avoid runtime checks for those invariants when they are proven.
  • You keep runtime code lean while still carrying strong compile-time guarantees.

Note: tactics are planned but not yet implemented. Today, proofs are written as explicit terms.

docs.title: FFI and Unsafe
docs.text: Just like Rust, LRL has an unsafe keyword that allows you to bypass certain checks.

docs.title: Unsafe
docs.text:
unsafe blocks allow you to: - Call extern functions (FFI). - Dereference raw pointers. - Implement unsafe traits.

(unsafe
  (call-external-function args))

docs.title: Foreign Function Interface (FFI)
docs.text:
LRL can link against C ABI libraries.

(extern "C" {
  (def put-char (-> Int Int))
})

docs.title: Safe Wrappers
docs.text:
The idiomatic way to handle unsafe code is to wrap it in a safe interface that enforces the invariants that the compiler can't check.

(def print-secure (-> String Unit)
  (lam s String
    (unsafe
       ;; ... low level implementation ...
       unit)))

docs.title: Performance Model
docs.text:
LRL compiles to native code via Rust.

  • Erasure: Everything in Prop is erased.
  • Monomorphization: Generic functions are typically monomorphized (like Rust), leading to efficient code but larger binaries.
  • Reference Counting: Currently, some structures may use RC, but the goal is affine types minimizing this overhead.

docs.title: Proof-Carrying API Without Runtime Proof Cost
docs.text:
(def with-self-eq
  (pi n Nat (pi p (Eq Nat n n) Nat))
  (lam n Nat
    (lam p (Eq Nat n n)
      (add n n))))

(def entry Nat
  (with-self-eq (succ (succ zero))
                (refl Nat (succ (succ zero)))))

p is checked by the type checker but erased at runtime.

docs.title: Predictable Structural Cost
docs.text:
(def sum-list (pi xs (List Nat) Nat)
  (lam xs (List Nat)
    (match xs Nat
      (case (nil) zero)
      (case (cons h t ih) (add h ih)))))

sum-list does one recursive step per element. No hidden tracing GC pauses are introduced by this definition pattern.

docs.title: Inspecting Generated Code
docs.text:
If you compile with: 

cargo run -p cli -- compile file.lrl -o out --backend typed
The compiler currently generates an intermediate Rust file output.rs in build/. You can inspect this to see exactly what LRL is producing.

Useful companions while debugging:

cargo run -p cli -- compile-mir file.lrl
cargo run -p cli -- --expand-full file.lrl
  • compile-mir helps verify borrow/lifetime lowering.
  • --expand-full lets you inspect macro output before type checking.

docs.text:
• Indent: 2 spaces.
  • Line Length: 80-100 characters.
  • Parentheses: Don't leave dangling parentheses.

  • Bad: (list 1 2 3 )

docs.title: Macro Discipline
docs.text: Don't use macros just because you can. - Use Functions when possible. They are easier to type-check and debug. - Use Macros for control flow (like if, match), binding forms, or DSLs.

docs.title: Proofs
docs.text: Keep proofs separate from logic where possible, or use the Prop universe to ensure they don't impact runtime performance.

docs.title: Why is inference limited?
docs.text: Full type inference for dependent types is undecidable. LRL relies on bidirectional typing, which requires annotations in top-level definitions and some other places, but infers types for most expressions.

docs.title: Why can't types depend on partial code?
docs.text: If a type depends on a function that loops forever, the type checker would loop forever. Logic requires total functions.

docs.title: Why does borrow checking exist if we transpile to Rust?
docs.text: LRL's borrow checker runs on MIR before codegen. It mirrors Rust's rules to ensure that the generated Rust code is valid and safe, providing error messages in terms of LRL source code rather than confusing Rust compiler errors.

docs.title: How do I do dynamic stuff?
docs.text: Use the Dyn type or Any. We support a "dynamic backend" which is more permissive, but the "typed backend" enforces static discipline.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
• Kernel: The trusted core component that verifies fully elaborated terms.
  • Elaboration: The process of converting surface syntax (with implicit arguments) into fully explicit core terms.
  • Definitional Equality: Two terms are definitionally equal if they reduce to the same form.
  • Prop: The universe of propositions. Elements are proofs and are erased at runtime.
  • Type: The universe of types. Elements are data and are preserved at runtime (mostly).
  • Motive: The return type function for a recursor/match expression.
  • Eliminator: A function that destructs an inductive value (like Nat.rec).
  • MIR: Mid-level Intermediate Representation. A control-flow graph representation used for optimizations and borrow checking.
  • Region: A static scope in the program (lifetime).
  • Hygiene: The property of macros that prevents accidental variable capture.
  • Staging: The separation of compile-time (macro expansion) and runtime execution.
  • Capability: A token representing permission to perform an effect.

docs.title: Compiler Architecture (Deterministic IDs + Pipeline Spine)
docs.text: This document captures architectural invariants needed for typed backends and stable builds.

docs.title: Deterministic ID Registry
docs.text:
A single registry mints nominal IDs during declaration loading/elaboration. IDs are derived from: - PackageId (name + version + source + hash) - ModulePath - ItemName - Disambiguator (only when required)

Definitions: - DefId: top-level definition (functions, constants, axioms) - AdtId: inductive type definition - CtorId: (AdtId, ctor_index) - FieldId: (CtorId, field_index)

Rules: - IDs are deterministic and build-stable. - IDs are not minted in MIR passes. - No semantic pass (borrowck/codegen/typing) depends on raw strings.

docs.title: Phase Spine (Single Pipeline)
docs.text:
Source → parse → macro-expand → elaborate → kernel check → lower to MIR → NLL borrow check → codegen

Notes: - Macros are syntax-only and do not mint semantic IDs. - Elaboration resolves identifiers and assigns DefId/AdtId/CtorId/FieldId. - MIR and downstream passes consume IDs and metadata only.

docs.title: Runtime Layout Policy
docs.text: Dependent indices do not affect runtime layout. Runtime-dependent indices must be explicit fields in the runtime representation.

docs.title: Interior Mutability Policy
docs.text: Interior mutability is expressed by marker traits/attributes resolved to DefId-based flags during elaboration. The panic-free profile rejects any interior mutability (RefCell/Mutex/Atomic).

docs.title: Sanity Rule
docs.text: Borrow checking, MIR typing, and codegen must never depend on raw strings for semantic identity. All semantics are keyed by IDs (including PackageId).

docs.title: MIR Semantic Truth (for this subset)

A program is in conformance when all of the following hold after MIR validation (typing + ownership + NLL):

  1. The same validated MIR is used for both backends.
  2. Observable behavior matches expected semantics:
  3. Exit code matches expected exit code.
  4. Canonical final result matches expected result (nat:N or bool:true|false).
  5. Non-result stdout lines match exactly.
  6. Dynamic and typed backend observables are identical for the same MIR.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Define a concrete, testable roadmap to move from a prelude-centric alpha setup to a real standard library with:

  • one public API contract (prelude_api)
  • tiny backend platform shims (prelude_impl_dynamic, prelude_impl_typed)
  • shared backend-neutral stdlib modules for user-facing logic
  • compact, readable syntax conventions suitable for day-to-day programming

This plan assumes current backend architecture and ownership/type/NLL rules remain authoritative.

docs.title: Current Baseline (as of this plan)
docs.text:
• Prelude architecture already exists:
  • stdlib/prelude_api.lrl (public contract)
  • stdlib/prelude_impl_dynamic.lrl (dynamic platform layer)
  • stdlib/prelude_impl_typed.lrl (typed platform layer)
  • Shared API contains core types/functions (Nat, Bool, List, add, append, etc.).
  • Platform layers are small and mostly runtime-boundary definitions (Dyn, EvalCap, eval).
  • Function application already accepts multiple arguments in one form:
  • (f a b c) parses/desugars as chained application.
  • Function definition type/binder syntax is still mostly unary/curried at core level:
  • explicit nested lam/pi style remains canonical.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Single public contract
  2. User code targets API names/types, not backend-specific files.

  3. No user program should import or depend on prelude_impl_*.

  4. One stdlib, two tiny platforms

  5. Shared algorithms live once under stdlib/std/*.

  6. prelude_impl_dynamic.lrl and prelude_impl_typed.lrl stay platform-only.

  7. Backend-neutral semantics first

  8. Any function in shared stdlib must compile under both backends.

  9. Differences are allowed only for explicitly documented platform boundaries.

  10. Strictly test-driven migration

  11. Every moved/added stdlib function gets compile + behavior checks.

  12. Conformance tests gate dynamic/typed parity for overlap subset.

  13. Syntax compactness without semantic shortcuts

  14. Keep core calculus unchanged (curried semantics).
  15. Add/desugar ergonomic sugar to reduce boilerplate where safe.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: The LeanRustLisp (LRL) compiler is structured as a pipeline of distinct crates, each with a specific responsibility. This separation is crucial for the "trusted kernel" architecture.

docs.title: High-Level Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Source (.lrl) is parsed into a Syntax Tree (frontend).
  2. Macros are expanded to produce a fully expanded Syntax Tree (frontend).
  3. Desugaring converts Syntax to Surface Terms (frontend).
  4. Elaboration converts Surface Terms to Core Terms (kernel), handling type inference and implicit arguments.
  5. Kernel verifies the Core Terms (type checking, definitional equality).
  6. MIR Lowering converts Core Terms to Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) (mir).
  7. Borrow Checking enforces ownership and lifetimes on MIR (mir).
  8. Codegen translates MIR to target code (Rust/Binary) (codegen).

docs.title: kernel (The Trusted Base)
docs.text:
• Role: The minimal, trusted core that verifies the correctness of the program.
  • Key Modules:
  • ast: Defines the Core Calculus (terms, inductives, universes).
  • checker: Implements type checking rules.
  • nbe: Normalization by Evaluation (for definitional equality).
  • ownership: Core ownership definitions.

docs.title: frontend (Untrusted)
docs.text:
• Role: User-facing features, parsing, and elaborating into the core.
  • Key Modules:
  • parser: S-expression parser.
  • macro_expander: Hygienic macro system implementation.
  • elaborator: Type inference and bidirectional typing to produce Core Terms.
  • diagnostics: Error reporting.

docs.title: mir (Optimization & Safety)
docs.text:
• Role: Intermediate representation for analysis and optimization.
  • Key Features:
  • Control-flow graph construction.
  • Borrow checker (NLL-style).
  • Optimizations.

docs.title: codegen (Backend)
docs.text:
• Role: Emitting executable code.
  • Targets:
  • Rust (transpilation).
  • LLVM (future).

docs.title: cli (Driver)
docs.text:
• Role: Command-line interface and REPL.
  • Features:
  • Orchestrates the pipeline.
  • Manages compiler flags and modes.

docs.title: Data Structures
docs.text:
• Syntax: frontend::surface::Syntax (S-expressions with spans).
  • SurfaceTerm: frontend::surface::Term (Desugared, unresolved names).
  • CoreTerm: kernel::ast::Term (Fully explicit, dependently typed calculus).
  • Env: kernel::checker::Env (Global environment of definitions and inductives).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The codegen crate translates MIR to Rust.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Lowering: MIR types/statements -> Rust AST.
  2. Runtime Support: Linking against lrl_rt (runtime library) which provides Nat, closures, etc.
  3. Output: Generates a .rs file which is then compiled by rustc.

docs.title: Erasure
docs.text: Ensure Prop elements are erased to () or dropped entirely.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The elaborator in frontend/src/elaborator.rs converts surface syntax into kernel terms.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
1. Name Resolution: Managing scopes and resolving identifiers.
  2. Type Inference: Generating metavariables (?m) for holes and solving them via unification.
  3. Implicit Arguments: Inserting code for implicit arguments.
  4. Desugaring: Converting match to Rec applications.

docs.title: Unification
docs.text: Bidirectional unification is used. If unification fails, an error is reported with distinct expected vs actual types.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The kernel crate is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB).

docs.title: Key Modules
docs.text:
• ast.rs: Core term definitions (Term, Level).
  • checker.rs: Type checker and definitional equality (def_eq).
  • nbe.rs: Normalization by Evaluation (the engine for def_eq).
  • inductives.rs: Inductive type validity checks (positivity, universe levels).

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Use LRL_DEFEQ_FUEL to adjust the fuel limit if the kernel seems to hang (which implies a non-terminating reduction or huge term).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Macro expansion happens before elaboration.

docs.title: Mechanism
docs.text:
1. The parser produces a Syntax tree.
  2. The expander traverses the tree.
  3. If it encounters a macro, it invokes the macro function (interpreted).
  4. Hygiene is maintained by tracking ScopeIds on syntax nodes.

docs.title: Adding Macros
docs.text: Macros are defined in standard libraries or user code. The expander must be able to load these definitions (bootstrapping).

docs.title: MIR
docs.text: Mid-level IR used for optimization and borrow checking. - Constructed from elaborated terms. - Explicit control flow (CFG).

docs.title: Bytecode (BC)
docs.text:
Interpreter bytecode used for: - REPL execution. - Macro expansion. - const evaluation.

The BC virtual machine is distinct from the compiled output.

docs.title: Test Suites
docs.text:
• cargo test: Unit tests for Rust components.
  • tests/*.lrl: Integration tests compiled by the CLI.
  • compile_test.lrl: Basic compilation check.

docs.title: Adding Tests
docs.text:
1. Create a new .lrl file in tests/.
  2. Add a RUN directive or similar harness (if applicable) or verify it compiles via cargo run -p cli -- compile tests/new_test.lrl.

docs.title: Trusted Computing Base (TCB)
docs.text: In LeanRustLisp, the correctness of the entire system relies on a small set of core components known as the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). If the TCB is correct, then all checked programs are type-safe and adhere to the language's logical consistency.

docs.title: The Kernel
docs.text:
The primary component of the TCB is the kernel crate.

  • Type Checker: The rules for type checking (Dependent Pi, Inductives, Sorts) are implemented here.
  • Definitional Equality: The logic for determining if two terms are definitionally equal (beta-reduction, etc.) must be correct.
  • Inductive Validity: The checks for positivity and universe consistency for new inductive types.

docs.title: What is NOT Trusted
docs.text:
• Frontend: The parser, macro expander, and elaborator are not trusted. If they produce an invalid Core Term, the Kernel will reject it.
  • Type Inference: Inference heuristics in the elaborator are a convenience; the result is always verified by the Kernel.

docs.title: Auditing
docs.text: Changes to the kernel directory should be audited with extreme care.

docs.title: LeanRustLisp Reference
docs.text:
This section provides the normative definition of the LeanRustLisp language.

Version: 0.1 Alpha

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text: Implementations MUST adhere to the rules in this section. If the behavior of the compiler contradicts this reference, it is a bug in the compiler (unless this reference is outdated, which is also a bug).

docs.title: Formal Specification
docs.text: For the mathematical definitions of the core calculus, see the Spec.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: LRL provides primitives for safe concurrency, relying on the type system to prevent data races.

docs.title: Primitives
docs.text: Concurrency support is provided by runtime primitives marked with specific attributes: - concurrency_primitive: Mutexes, Channels. - atomic_primitive: Atomic integers/booleans.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The type system (and future Send/Sync traits) ensures that mutable data cannot be shared across threads without synchronization (Mutex). - Interior Mutability: Types like RefCell or Mutex allow mutation through shared references (&T). - Markers: The kernel tracks interior mutability via the interior_mutable marker to ensure Copy safety (types with interior mutability cannot be trivially Copy unless safe).

docs.title: Definitional Equality
docs.text: Definitional equality is the equivalence relation used by the type checker.

docs.title: Reductions
docs.text:
• Beta (β): Function application. (\x. b) a ≡ b[x/a].
  • Delta (δ): Constant unfolding. If def x := v, then x ≡ v.
  • Unfolding is controlled by Transparency. Opaque definitions are not unfolded.
  • Fuel: The checker uses a fuel metric to prevent infinite loops during unfolding of partial or cyclic terms.
  • Iota (ι): Inductive elimination. The application of a recursor Rec to a constructor Ctor reduces to the corresponding minor premise.
  • Eta (η): Extensionality. (\x. f x) ≡ f.
  • Zeta (ζ): Let-expansion. let x := v in b ≡ b[x/v].

docs.title: Totality
docs.text: Only Total definitions are legally unfolded during type checking. Partial definitions cannot be unfolded (to prevent unsoundness/loops in the type checker).

docs.title: Kernel (Kxxxx)
docs.text: Errors dealing with the core logic and type system. - K0001: Unknown variable. - K0002: Type mismatch. - K0005: Unknown inductive. - K0015: Non-positive inductive occurrence. - K0018: Non-terminating recursion. - K0021: Ownership violation.

docs.title: Frontend (Fxxxx)
docs.text: Errors in parsing or elaboration. - F0001: Unexpected EOF. - F0200: Unbound variable. - F0202: Ambiguous constructor. - F0211: Non-exhaustive match.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
• --trace-macros: Print macro expansion steps.
  • --trace-elaboration: Print elaboration trace.
  • -D <code/category>: Deny warning.
  • -A <code/category>: Allow warning.

docs.title: Elaboration
docs.text: Elaboration is the process of converting the user-friendly surface syntax into the fully explicit core calculus.

docs.title: Type Inference
docs.text:
LRL uses bidirectional type checking. - Inference: Computing the type of a term from its structure. - Checking: Verifying a term against a known expected type.

Top-level definitions (def name type val) are checked against the provided signature.

docs.title: Holes (_)
docs.text:
The underscore _ allows you to ask the compiler to infer a term or type. - In expressions: (cons 1 _) (infers the tail is nil/empty if constrained). - In types: (Vec _ n) (infers the element type).

If the elaborator cannot solve a hole (unresolved metavariable), it reports an error.

docs.title: Implicit Arguments
docs.text: Functions declare implicit binders with braces ((pi {A (sort 1)} ...), (lam {A} (sort 1) ...)). At a call site the elaborator inserts a metavariable for each implicit argument that is not given explicitly ({arg} gives it explicitly) and solves it by unification with the types of the explicit arguments and the expected type. This works in values, in the types of definitions (also under binders, e.g. (pi n Nat (Eq Nat (idn n) n))), in match scrutinees and in explicit (motive ...) clauses. A constraint that cannot be decided yet (for example pred ?n =?= m, or min1 ?k =?= succ zero with a definition applied to an unsolved metavariable) is postponed and retried, with every solved metavariable substituted, once the other arguments and the expected type have been checked; constraints that stay blocked are reported as F0217 (unsolved constraints), and constraints that turn out to be false as type errors (F0214/F0205). Different constructors never unify, whatever metavariables appear below them (zero =?= succ ?n fails at once with F0214).

docs.title: Foreign Function Interface
docs.text: Interfacing with other languages.

docs.title: Extern Blocks
docs.text:
Primitive constants can be declared without value.

(def my-c-func (-> Int Int))

To actually link, these must be mapped to native symbols in the backend.

docs.title: Unsafe
docs.text:
Calling foreign functions is generally unsafe because the FFI cannot guarantee LRL's invariants (validity, total functions, etc).

unsafe blocks allow: - Calling external primitives. - Bypassing some memory safety checks.

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text:
This EBNF describes the surface syntax (S-expressions) produced by the parser.

program ::= expression*

expression ::= atom
             | list
             | braced_list
             | quote
             | quasiquote
             | unquote
             | unquote_splicing
             | index_expr

atom ::= INTEGER | STRING | SYMBOL | HOLE

list ::= '(' expression* ')'

braced_list ::= '{' expression* '}'

quote ::= "'" expression

quasiquote ::= "`" expression

unquote ::= "," expression

unquote_splicing ::= ",@" expression

index_expr ::= expression '[' expression ']' 
/* Parsed as (kind: Index, expr, index) */

INTEGER ::= [0-9]+
STRING  ::= '"' (CHARS | ESCAPE)* '"'
HOLE    ::= "_"
SYMBOL  ::= [^ \t\n\r()\[\]{}"',`]+  /* excluding HOLE */

docs.title: Inductives
docs.text: Inductive reference.

docs.title: Declaration
docs.text:
(inductive Name (Sort u)
  (ctor1 (-> Arg1 Name))
  ...)

docs.title: Universes
docs.text: Inductives can live in Prop or Type u. - Prop Inductives: Must not have large elimination (cannot eliminate to Type unless singleton/empty). - Strict Positivity: Recursive occurrences of the inductive type in constructors must be strictly positive (nested to the left of arrows).

docs.title: Eliminators
docs.text: For every inductive T, the kernel generates a recursor T.rec. Surface match expressions are elaborated into applications of T.rec.

docs.title: Input/Output
docs.text: LRL encapsulates side effects.

docs.title: The IO Type
docs.text: IO A is a primitive opaque type representing a computation that performs effects and produces an A.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
The main function must have type IO Unit. The runtime executes this action.

(Note: The current IO model is a placeholder. Future versions may use algebraic effects or monad transformers).

docs.title: Lexical Structure
docs.text: LRL source files must be UTF-8 encoded.

docs.title: Whitespace
docs.text: Whitespace is defined as any character for which char::is_whitespace() returns true (includes spaces, tabs, newlines). Whitespace separates tokens but is otherwise ignored.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
Comments start with ; and extend to the end of the line.

; This is a comment
(add 1 2) ; Comment at end of line

docs.title: Identifiers (Symbols)
docs.text:
Symbols are sequences of characters that are NOT: - Whitespace - Delimiters: (, ), [, ], {, } - Quotes: ', `, ,

Examples: foo, foo-bar, +, ->, Foo.Bar.

Note: The symbol _ is reserved as a "Hole".

docs.title: Integers
docs.text: Currently, only unsigned integers fitting in usize are supported by the parser. Regex: [0-9]+

docs.title: Strings
docs.text: Strings are enclosed in double quotes ". Supported escapes: - \n (newline) - \r (carriage return) - \t (tab) - \" (quote) - \\ (backslash)

docs.title: Delimiters
docs.text:
• (...): Standard lists (S-expressions).
  • {...}: Braced lists (often used for implicit arguments or blocks, semantically equivalent to lists at parse time).
  • [...]: Indexing (postfix). a[b] parses as (index a b).

docs.title: Macro System
docs.text:
LRL provides template macros that operate on syntax objects (Syntax):

(defmacro name (p1 ... pn) template)

A call (name a1 ... an) (exactly n arguments) is replaced by template with every symbol pi replaced by the argument syntax ai; the result is expanded again. Quasiquote (`, ,, ,@) may be used inside templates to build syntax. Nothing is evaluated at macro time: there are no conditionals, no pattern matching on arguments and no syntax primitives. The full specification is docs/spec/macro_system.md.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text: Macro expansion happens before desugaring and type checking. It needs no interpreter: it is substitution into templates. Macro output is ordinary surface syntax and goes through the whole pipeline (elaboration, kernel, MIR), so a macro cannot produce anything that could not be written by hand.

docs.title: Hygiene
docs.text:
Hygiene covers local binders: - Syntax introduced by a macro template is marked with a fresh scope for each call. - Arguments passed to a macro keep their original scopes.

So a binder introduced by a template does not capture a variable of the caller, and a reference introduced by a template does not resolve to a local binder of the caller.

Macro names and global names (definitions, constructors, inductive types) are not hygienic: they are resolved by name where the macro is used. There is no API to break hygiene on purpose (no datum->syntax). See docs/spec/macros/hygiene.md.

docs.title: Expansion Order
docs.text: Macros are expanded outside-in (top-down); the arguments of a macro call are not expanded before the call (they are expanded when the instantiated template is expanded). Expansion is bounded (number of invocations per top-level form, nesting depth) and repeated identical calls are reported as cycles.

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text: Macro expansion is deterministic. The same input source code produces the same output syntax tree.

docs.title: Files as Modules
docs.text: Every .lrl file is a module. The module name is derived from the filename.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text: (Future Specification) Packages will be managed by a package manager (likely integrated into the CLI), defining dependencies and workspaces.

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: Currently, top-level definitions in a module are visible to any module that imports it. (Future: private / pub visibility modifiers).

docs.title: Name Resolution
docs.text: LRL allows breaking programs into modules (files) and managing namespaces.

docs.title: Scoping Rules
docs.text: Scopes are lexical. Local variables shadow outer variables. Definitions in the same module are visible everywhere in that module (order-independent for top-level def, though the kernel requires valid dependency ordering).

docs.title: Modules and Imports
docs.text: Each file is a module. - use <module> opens a module, making its definitions available unqualified. - use <module> as <alias> adds a qualified alias.

docs.title: Ambiguity
docs.text: If two opened modules export the same name, using that name unqualified is an error (AmbiguousName). You must use the qualified name Module.name.

docs.title: Ownership and Borrowing
docs.text: LRL enforces affine usage of linear resources.

docs.title: Usage Modes
docs.text: The system tracks variable usage in three modes: 1. Consuming: The value is moved. It cannot be used again. 2. MutBorrow: The value is mutably borrowed. Exclusive access. 3. Observational: The value is read. Shared access.

docs.title: Move Semantics
docs.text: By default, passing a non-Copy value to a function (f x) is a move (Consuming usage). Subsequent use of x is a compile-time error (UseAfterMove).

docs.title: Copy Types
docs.text: Types like Nat and Bool are Copy. They can be used multiple times; each usage is a copy.

docs.title: Closures and Capture
docs.text: Closures capture variables from their environment. The capture mode is inferred based on usage in the body. Code that attempts to capture a moved variable is rejected.

docs.title: Pattern Matching
docs.text:
Pattern matching is a surface-level feature that compiles to recursors. The precise syntax is in docs/spec/syntax_contract_0_1.md ("(match ...)").

(match scrutinee ReturnType (case (Ctor x1 ... xk) body) ...)      ; constant motive
(match scrutinee (motive M) (case (Ctor x1 ... xk) body) ...)      ; explicit dependent motive

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text: A pattern is one constructor applied to variables: the constructor's explicit fields in order, each recursive field followed by its induction hypothesis ((case (succ k ih) ...)). Patterns are not nested; nested matching is written with nested match.

docs.title: Exhaustiveness
docs.text: A match must have exactly one case per constructor of the inductive type. Missing, duplicate or unknown cases are compile-time errors. Cases that are impossible for the scrutinee's indices must still be written (against the motive, e.g. returning a unit value).

docs.title: Motives
docs.text: With a constant return type, every case and the whole match have that type. With (motive M), M is a function over the scrutinee type's indices and the scrutinee, returning a sort; each case is checked against M at its constructor's indices and value, induction hypotheses have type M at the recursive field, and the match has type M at the scrutinee's indices and the scrutinee. This is how dependent results are written (a total head on Vec A (succ n), append with result length add n m, proofs by induction).

docs.title: Compilation
docs.text: A match elaborates to one application of the inductive's recursor (Rec): parameters, motive, one minor premise per case (a function of the pattern variables), the scrutinee's indices and the scrutinee. Recursion happens only through induction hypotheses, so every match is structurally recursive; general recursion needs fix in a partial definition.

docs.title: Data Representation
docs.text:
• Nat: Arbitrary precision integers (BigInt).
  • Inductives: Tagged unions or struct pointers.
  • Closures: (Result, Environment) pairs.

docs.title: Erasure
docs.text: The compiler performs full erasure of: - Prop types and values. - Type parameters (polymorphism is monomorphized or erased depending on backend). - PhantomData.

docs.title: Memory Management
docs.text: LRL uses Affine Types to minimize GC. - Unique data is managed manually (drop flags). - Shared data may use Reference Counting (Ref/Shared).

docs.title: Standard Library Reference
docs.text: The LeanRustLisp standard library provides core types, data structures, and algorithms for building verified software.

stdlib/
├── prelude_api.lrl          # Public API contract (all backends)
├── prelude_impl_dynamic.lrl # Dynamic backend platform layer
├── prelude_impl_typed.lrl   # Typed backend platform layer
└── std/
    ├── core/                # Primitives: Bool, Nat, Int, Float
    ├── data/                # Collections: List, Option, Result, Pair
    └── control/             # Effects: Comp

Important: User code should target prelude_api only. Never import prelude_impl_* directly.

docs.title: Type System
docs.text: The core of LRL is a Calculus of Inductive Constructions (CIC).

docs.title: Universes
docs.text:
There is a hierarchy of universes: - Prop (Sort 0): Logical propositions. Erased at runtime. - Type 0 (Sort 1): Basics types (Nat, Bool). - Type n (Sort n+1): Higher universes.

Prop is impredicative. Type levels are predicative.

docs.title: Dependent Products (Pi)
docs.text: The fundamental type constructor is Pi (Π). forall (x : A), B x. If B is constant, this is A -> B.

docs.title: Definitional Equality
docs.text:
Two terms are definitionally equal if they compute to the same normal form. The kernel checks this by normalizing both terms (with limits on "fuel").

Reductions: - Beta: (\x. b) a ~~> b[x/a] - Delta: def x := v -> x ~~> v - Iota: Recursor reduction (pattern matching). - Eta: (\x. f x) ~~> f (for functions).

docs.title: Inductive Types
docs.text: Inductive types are defined by their introduction rules (constructors). Their elimination rule (recursor) is automatically generated. Recursion must be well-founded (guarded by structural decrease or a measure).

docs.title: Unsafe
docs.text: LRL allows bypassing safety checks in designated blocks.

docs.title: The unsafe keyword
docs.text: The unsafe block allows: - Dereferencing raw pointers. - Calling functions marked unsafe (including FFI). - Implementing unsafe traits.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text: It is the programmer's responsibility to ensure that unsafe code maintains the logical invariants of the system: - Memory safety (no invalid pointers). - Type safety (casting must be valid). - Thread safety (no data races).

docs.title: Language Versions
docs.text:
LRL follows semantic versioning.

  • Major: Breaking changes to the core calculus or surface syntax.
  • Minor: New features, backwards-compatible additions.
  • Patch: Bug fixes.

docs.title: Stability Guarantees
docs.text: As of 0.1 Alpha: - No stability guarantees are provided. Syntax and features may change breakingly between commits.

docs.title: Editions
docs.text: Future versions may support "Editions" (like Rust) to allow breaking syntactic changes while maintaining compatibility for old code.

docs.title: 1. Kernel Calculus Base
docs.text: The kernel is based on the Calculus of Inductive Constructions (CIC) dependent type theory, closely aligned with Lean's kernel.

docs.title: 2. Universes
docs.text:
• Prop (Sort 0): The universe of computationally irrelevant propositions.
    • Impredicative: Prop is impredicative. The universe level of a Pi-type Π (x : A), B is Prop if B : Prop, regardless of the universe of A.
    • Erasure: Terms in Prop are proofs and are erased at runtime.
  • Type u (Sort u+1): A hierarchy of computational types, indexed by universe levels u. It is not cumulative: a type in Sort u is not accepted where a type in a larger sort is expected.
    • Predicative: The universe level of Π (x : A), B where B : Type v is max(level(A), v).
  • Binder types are types: in Π (x : A), B both A and B must be types (their types reduce to a sort), and the binder type of λ, let and fix must be a type; the kernel reports K0004 (ExpectedSort) otherwise (an opaque alias of a sort counts as a sort).

docs.title: 3. Function Kinds (Ownership)
docs.text:
Pi and Lam carry a function-kind annotation (Fn, FnMut, FnOnce) that controls ownership and call semantics for runtime values. The kind is part of type identity (no definitional equality across kinds). Beta reduction is unchanged. See docs/spec/function_kinds.md for the full specification.

Core grammar excerpt:

FnKind ::= Fn | FnMut | FnOnce
Pi(ty, body, binder_info, fn_kind)
Lam(ty, body, binder_info, fn_kind)

docs.title: 4. Inductive Types and Elimination
docs.text:
The kernel supports inductive definitions.

  • Well-formed declarations: the arity must be a type Π (x1 : A1) ... (xn : An), S whose binders are written out and whose result S is a sort, or an alias (e.g. an opaque definition) that unfolds to one; every constructor type must be a type, i.e. its binder types are types and its result applies the inductive to arguments of the arity's binder types. Violations are K0004 (ExpectedSort) or a type mismatch. (Without these checks an arity such as an empty proposition, Bot : False, made Bot itself a closed proof of False.) The universe check of constructor fields uses the unfolded result sort when the arity is written through an alias.
  • Zeta expansion first: the kernel reads the arity and the constructor types syntactically (parameter inference, strict positivity, nested occurrences, the recursive arguments of the recursor and of ι-reduction, Copy derivation), so it first replaces every let in them by its value (zeta reduction, part of definitional equality); the declaration is stored in that form. A let-bound variable therefore cannot hide an occurrence of the inductive, and a field written (let Y (sort 1) L Y) in an inductive L is a recursive argument with an induction hypothesis.
  • Strict positivity (as in Lean 4 and Coq): in a constructor field the inductive being declared may occur only as the head of the field type, or of the codomain of a Pi in it, applied to its own parameters (a field Nat -> T of T is fine); it must not occur in the domain of a Pi, at any depth. Violations are K0015 (NonPositiveOccurrence). Occurrences as an argument of another type (List T) are nested inductives, which are not supported (K0016). The inductive also may not occur in the arguments (parameters or indices) of a constructor's result type (as in Lean 4 and Coq): (inductive T (pi P (sort 0) (sort 0)) (ctor base (T (pi x (T Tru) False)))) is rejected with K0015 (InductiveInCtorResultArg).
    • (ctor mk (pi f (pi x Bad False) Bad)) is rejected (a negative occurrence gives omega := λ b. unroll b b and a closed proof of False by omega (mk omega)), and so is the same field written (let X (sort 0) Bad (pi x X False)).
    • An occurrence under two arrows, (ctor intro (pi g (pi p (pi a A (sort 0)) (sort 0)) A)) (intro : ((A -> Prop) -> Prop) -> A), is positive but not strictly positive and is rejected: with the impredicative Prop, f P := intro (λ Q. P = Q) is injective, and the diagonal predicate W x := ∃ P. f P = x ∧ ¬ P x gives a closed proof of False (Coquand–Paulin).
  • Failed declarations leave nothing behind: a declaration rejected by any check, including a failed copy derivation (K0029), is not registered (not even as an empty type), so its name can be declared again.
  • Universe rule for constructor fields (as in Lean 4 and Coq): if the arity ends in Sort u with u not Prop, every constructor field (x : A) must have a type in a universe at most u: A : Sort v with v ≤ u. The fields are the binders of a constructor type after the inductive's uniform parameters (constructor types repeat the parameters as their leading binders). The level v is the sort of the inferred type of A, so a field of type Sort l has level l+1 (Sort l : Sort (l+1)) and a field of type Π (x : Nat), Sort 1 has level 2. Violations are K0017 (UniverseLevelTooSmall). Surface programs write only concrete levels ((sort n)); for declarations with universe-level parameters (kernel API), v ≤ u must hold for every assignment of the parameters (Lean 4's comparison: u+1 ≤ max u v + 1 holds, 1 ≤ imax 1 u does not, since u may be 0), and level normalisation keeps imax a u distinct from max a u when u may be 0. Level normalisation writes max (a+1) (b+1) as (max a b)+1; the comparison distributes the successor over max again ((max a b)+k = max (a+k) (b+k)), so that, as in Lean 4, u+1 ≤ max u v + 2 holds.
    • Example: (inductive U (sort 1) (ctor mkU (pi A (sort 1) U))) is rejected: its field has a type of level 2. Accepting it would let El : U -> (sort 1) (by match) satisfy El (mkU A) ≡ A, i.e. make (sort 1) a retract of a type in (sort 1), the setting of Hurkens' paradox for Type : Type. Declared in (sort 2) it is accepted (a retract of (sort 1) in a larger universe is harmless).
    • Parameters and indices of the arity are not constrained (Lean 4 and Coq do not constrain them either): a parameter is not stored in the value and an index is determined by the value's type. (inductive T (pi A (sort 1) (sort 1)) (ctor mkT (T Nat))), a family indexed by a type, lives in (sort 1), and so may an inductive with a parameter A : (sort 2) (its fields must still fit: a field of type A has level 2 and is rejected in a (sort 1) inductive).
    • Inductive propositions (u = Prop) are not constrained: a proposition may have a field of type (sort 1); what it may be eliminated into is governed by the elimination restriction below (such a proposition is not large-eliminable).
    • The universe hierarchy is not cumulative, so the rule also means that a value of a large inductive (e.g. the prelude's Comp A, which lives in (sort 2) because its constructors store types, see prelude_api.md) cannot be stored in, or passed as an argument of, something that expects a (sort 1) type.
  • Large Elimination Restriction: To maintain proof irrelevance, elimination from an inductive type in Prop to a type in Type u (where u > 0) is restricted. The restriction applies to every inductive that may be a proposition: one whose arity ends in a sort whose level is not provably nonzero for every assignment of the level parameters (Prop, and with level parameters, kernel API only, Sort u or Sort (imax 1 u); not Sort (u+1) or Sort (max 1 u)). As in Lean 4 this is decided once per declaration, so PU.{u} : Sort u with two constructors eliminates only into Prop, for every instantiation of u.
    • Allowed only if the inductive type has zero constructors (e.g., False) or one constructor all of whose fields are proofs (e.g., True, And). The fields are the constructor's binders after the inductive's uniform parameters; parameters are not restricted (a proposition Wrap (A : Type) with one constructor whose only field is a proof may be eliminated into Type). A field is a proof if its type is a proposition (the field type's own type is Prop). A field whose type is the sort Prop itself holds a proposition, not a proof, and blocks large elimination: otherwise (inductive PW (sort 0) (ctor mkpw (pi P (sort 0) PW))) would give up : PW -> Prop with up (mkpw P) ≡ P, making Prop a retract of a proposition, which is inconsistent with an impredicative Prop (Hurkens' paradox). Violations are K0027 (LargeElimination).
    • Exception: inductives matching the equality shape (A : Type u) -> (a : A) -> (b : A) -> Prop with refl : (A : Type u) -> (a : A) -> Eq A a a may eliminate into Type (transport/J), even though their parameters are in Type.
    • Elimination from Prop to Prop is always allowed.
  • Explicit Recursor Universes: Recursor terms must carry explicit universe levels (e.g., Rec Nat [u]). The kernel rejects Rec with missing levels. The elaborator computes the level from the motive type and supplies it.
  • Recursor type (minor premises and indices): the recursor's type binds, for each constructor, a minor premise. The minor premise binds the constructor's fields at their declared types, each recursive field immediately followed by its induction hypothesis (ih : C js x) (the motive at that field's indices and the field), and ends in the motive applied to the constructor's result indices and the constructor applied to its fields. Each type in this telescope — a later field's type, an induction-hypothesis index, a result index — is the constructor's own, read in the interleaved context: a reference to a field keeps its meaning, a reference to anything bound outside the fields is lifted over the induction hypotheses inserted before it. In particular a field whose type depends on an earlier field placed after a recursive field keeps that dependency (node : (r : T) (n : Nat) (v : Tag n) -> T gives the minor premise (r : T) (ih : C r) (n : Nat) (v : Tag n) -> C (node r n v), with v : Tag n, not Tag ih). ι-reduction (try_reduce_rec) applies the actual fields and the induction hypotheses in the same order, so the recursor type and ι-reduction agree and subject reduction holds. Likewise, in a family whose index telescope is dependent (D : (A : Sort 1) -> (x : A) -> Sort 1), each index binder in the recursor's main telescope keeps its reference to the earlier indices (x : A), not to the motive or a minor premise; the recursor type is well-formed and such a family can be eliminated.
  • Termination of total definitions (structural recursion): a recursive call must supply the decreasing argument, and that argument must be structurally smaller than the function's decreasing argument. "Smaller" means a field bound by a minor premise of a recursor whose major premise is the decreasing argument itself, or is already smaller than it — not a field of a recursor applied to an unrelated value (Rec Nat .. (succ n) does not make its field smaller than n), and never the induction hypothesis of a minor premise (the IH is the recursor's result on that field, not a subterm of the major premise). A call that stops before the decreasing argument is a partial application that could later be applied to any value and is rejected (MissingDecreasingArgument). These rules are enforced for definitions reaching the kernel through either surface syntax or the kernel API; without them a total definition could recurse on its own result and fail to terminate, from which a closed proof of an empty inductive (False) follows.

docs.title: 5. Definitional Equality and Unfolding
docs.text:
Definitional equality (a ≡ b) is decided by a Normalization-by-Evaluation (NbE) engine.

  • Transparency: Definitions carry a transparency hint.
    • Transparent (Reducible): The default. Unfolded during standard type checking.
    • Opaque (Irreducible): Unfolded only when explicitly requested (e.g., by tactics or specialized reduction modes), effectively abstracting the implementation details.
  • Reduction: Includes Beta (λ), Iota (recursion), Zeta (let), and Delta (definition unfolding based on transparency).
  • Default policy: Type checking uses transparency mode Reducible (respecting opaque).
  • Fuel / budget: Definitional equality, and the normalisation the type checker uses to expose Pi types and sorts (whnf, whnf_in_ctx), are fuel-bounded so that the kernel reports that it cannot decide instead of looping. The default fuel is 100_000, configurable via LRL_DEFEQ_FUEL or the CLI flag --defeq-fuel <N> (the CLI flag overrides the env var). The fuel is a budget for one check (one conversion problem, or one normalisation: its evaluation and its read-back share the budget), and every step is charged: δ (unfolding a definition), ι (a recursor step), β (applying a λ), ζ (a let), and every binder that read-back or comparison opens (instantiating a closure with a fresh variable). When fuel is exhausted, the kernel reports K0048 with context; marking large definitions as opaque reduces unfolding pressure. Closure environments are shared during evaluation, so the cost of a step does not grow with the size of the values it handles. Because every step counts, very small budgets no longer suffice for the prelude's own checks.
  • Depth limit: independently of the fuel, a fuelled evaluation, read-back or comparison may not nest deeper than nbe::MAX_EVAL_DEPTH (20_000) steps; deeper nesting reports K0056 (NormalizationDepthExceeded) instead of exhausting the native stack. The limit is sized for the CLI, which runs the compiler on a 1 GiB stack; a client of the kernel API must likewise run the checker on a large stack (on a default 8 MiB thread, a debug build overflows at a few thousand nested steps, e.g. a numeral succ^2000 zero in a type).
  • Fix unfolding: fix (general recursion) is never unfolded during type checking — neither by definitional equality nor by the normalisation that exposes a Pi type for an application (T-App), a sort, or a binder type. Applying a fixpoint there is reported as K0049 (DefEqFixUnfold). A term whose type can only be computed by unfolding a fixpoint (e.g. zero at the domain T zero of T := fix T (Nat -> Type) (λ m. Nat)) is rejected, and a fixpoint application that would never stop unfolding (inside a stuck recursor) is reported instead of exhausting the stack. Use partial for general recursion and opaque to keep it out of reductions in type checking.
  • Guarded unfolding of self-referential definitions: a total definition whose value refers to itself (structural recursion through its own constant: possible through the kernel API, or on the surface when --allow-redefine gives a name a new body that calls the old one) is unfolded only when it is applied to its decreasing argument (rec_arg, from the termination check) and that argument is a constructor application, as Coq does for fix. Otherwise the application stays stuck: unfolding it eagerly gave a stuck call such as add n zero an infinite normal form. Definitions that do not refer to themselves (e.g. written with match) are unfolded as before.
  • Safety classification: Prop classification respects opaque by default; explicit contexts can opt in to unfolding for checks like large elimination and Prop-in-data. MIR lowering may still peek through opaque aliases to detect Ref/interior mutability. These classification checks do not make opaque transparent for definitional equality.

docs.title: 6. Axioms and Classical Logic
docs.text:
The kernel supports classical logic via axioms (e.g., Excluded Middle, Choice).

  • Explicit Tracking: Axioms must be declared explicitly.
  • Explicit Classification: Axioms may carry tags (e.g., classical) that the kernel uses to classify dependencies; no name-based heuristics are used.
    • Surface syntax attaches tags via (axiom classical name ty) or (axiom (classical) name ty). Untagged axioms are treated as non-classical.
  • Dependency Tracking: Every definition tracks the set of axioms it depends on (transitively). This allows users to know if a theorem relies on classical logic or specific axioms.
  • import classical introduces the axiom classical_choice with type Π (P : Prop), ((P → False) → False) → P (double-negation elimination), tagged as classical.

docs.title: 7. Completeness & Totality
docs.text:
• Total Fragment: Definitions involved in types must be terminating.
    • Structural recursion (via Rec) or well-founded recursion (via Acc) is enforced.
    • General recursion (fix) is rejected in total definitions.
  • Partial Fragment: General recursion is allowed and cannot participate in definitional equality during type checking. Partial definitions must return an effect type (e.g., Comp A), and the kernel enforces this requirement.
    • fix is the only general-recursion form; it is permitted only in partial defs. A top-level expression may not contain fix either (C0008): expressions are evaluated for display, and a looping fixpoint there aborted the process.
    • T-Fix: fix f : A. t has type A when A is a type that reduces to a Pi type and t : A in the context extended with f : A — with A read in that extended context, i.e. weakened by one binder (the kernel and the elaborator used to check t against the unweakened A, so free variables of the annotation were read one binder off: an ill-typed body was accepted and a well-typed one rejected).
    • A fixpoint may not return a proof: the result type at the end of the fixpoint's Pi telescope must not be a proposition (K0055, FixProofCodomain). Proofs are erased at run time, so a looping fixpoint returning a proof is never run: (fix go (pi n Nat (Eq Nat (succ zero) zero)) (lam n Nat (go n))) stood for a proof of a false equation, and transport along it made compiled code use true as a Nat.

docs.title: 8. Definitions and Redefinition
docs.text:
• Values: only an axiom may be declared without a value (K0053, MissingDefinitionValue); every other definition is admitted on the strength of its checked value.
  • Axiom tracking is computed by the kernel: an axiom always depends on itself, whatever dependency list the client supplies, and its dependents inherit it (K0023 for a computable definition using it).
